title: SEC sues LSU, Lane Kiffin in federal court over push to add cut NFL players to roster
content:
The SEC filed a lawsuit in federal court against LSU, head football coach Lane Kiffin and other school administrators on Thursday as the conference and university remain at odds over the eligibility status of multiple potential LSU football players who spent time on NFL training camp rosters.

The SEC seeks a preliminary and permanent injunction prohibiting LSU from violating the conference’s First Amendment rights by forcing the conference to associate with actions that violate the conference’s rules. A similar legal argument was made by the Big 12 against Texas Tech in its federal filing earlier this summer around Brendan Sorsby. That case has yet to move forward, though the Big 12’s argument impacted Sorsby’s decision to leave Texas Tech and accept permanent ineligibility status from the NCAA.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Alabama, comes on the same day that a hearing is being held in Louisiana state court regarding a preliminary injunction that could determine the eligibility status of a number of athletes, including tight end Dae’Quan Wright and defensive tackle Zxavian Harris, former Ole Miss players under Kiffin. The hearing stems from a separate lawsuit against the NCAA involving Wright and Harris, who signed NFL contracts this offseason but are now fighting the NCAA’s new age-based eligibility rule and attempting to return to college football.

“Despite the SEC’s longstanding rules prohibiting professional athletes from returning to college athletics, Defendants saw this as an opportunity to be exploited,” the filing reads. “They began an orchestrated campaign to recruit professional athletes to join LSU’s football roster for the 2026-27 season.”

The SEC recently reemphasized and clarified an NCAA rule that prevents athletes who have signed professional contracts from returning to play in college football. According to the SEC’s lawsuit, LSU voted in favor of those actions. SEC commissioner Greg Sankey is expected to testify at the Thursday hearing in Louisiana on behalf of the SEC.

“Defendants have continued their campaign to engage in willful efforts to recruit and soon roster professional athletes in direct defiance of the Professionalism Rules,” the filing reads. “Defendants’ conduct has already harmed the Conference and threatens to cause further substantial harm if not curbed.”

The SEC previously indicated it will comply with the state court ruling in Louisiana, which could reinforce the immediate eligibility of Wright, Harris and roughly 30 other former college athletes. The SEC’s filing in federal court also states that it is not asking to have athletes declared ineligible but rather that the conference seeks to “disassociate from conduct that directly undermines” the conference.

Essentially, the SEC wants the ability to enforce rules and sanctions against its member schools as a way to deter LSU — or any other league school — from rostering and playing athletes who signed professional contracts after leaving college.

The NCAA recently simplified its eligibility rules, essentially giving every athlete five years to play five seasons. The change did not, however, apply to fourth-year seniors who had just completed their eligibility. That led to a wave of lawsuits from recruits in the 2022 high school class seeking an extra year.

No. 11 LSU plays Clemson in Baton Rouge on Saturday evening. Rosters must be finalized by the end of Friday.

This story will be updated.
